extracted.intended_audience: Class VI permit applicants, state/tribal UIC program regulators, and industry stakeholders (developers of CO2 capture, transport, and sequestration projects)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory preamble describing requirements, expectations, timelines, and supporting resources for applying for and administering Underground Injection Control (UIC) Class VI permits for geologic CO2 sequestration, and related expectations for CCS deployment on coal-fired units.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA Regions classification and project decision schedules
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA Regions are expected to classify all Class VI well applications received on or after December 12, 2023, as applications for major new UIC injection wells, which requires the Regions to develop project decision schedules for reviewing Class VI permit applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal guidelines include this classification expectation and require Regions to set project decision schedules and target timeframes for permit-review components (e.g., public comment periods, responses to comments, final permit decisions) to streamline and create uniformity in the Class VI permitting process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target timeframe for review of complete Class VI applications
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA aims to review complete Class VI applications and issue permits when appropriate within approximately 24 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 24-month timeframe is dependent on factors such as project complexity and the quality/completeness of the submitted application. Applicants should submit complete applications and respond to requests for information promptly to avoid extending review time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class VI permit tracker transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA maintains a Class VI permit tracker that shows information for projects that have submitted Class VI applications, including current permit review stage, NOD/RAI status, and applicant response time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants and stakeholders can use the tracker to monitor status; EPA noted most permits submitted within past 12 months and currently 44 projects (130 wells) under review. Tracker supports transparency and helps set expectations on review progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant responsibility for complete and timely submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must submit a complete application and provide any information requested by the permitting agency in a timely manner so as not to extend overall review time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When EPA receives incomplete or insufficient permit applications it issues Notices of Deficiency (NODs) or Requests for Additional Information (RAIs), waits for applicant responses, and then re-reviews — this back-and-forth can substantially delay permitting decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy application process for states
rubrics_metrics.description: States may apply to the EPA for primacy to administer Class VI programs; the primacy application process has four phases: (1) pre-application activities, (2) completeness review and determination, (3) application evaluation, and (4) rulemaking and codification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once primacy granted, EPA may transfer pending applications to the state. Primacy leverages state expertise and capacity to support efficient permit reviews; examples of granted primacy include North Dakota, Wyoming, and Louisiana.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of federal grants and capacity-building resources
rubrics_metrics.description: IIJA established a $50 million grant program to support states, Tribes, and territories in developing and implementing UIC Class VI programs; EPA has allocated funds to jurisdictions that submitted letters of intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA also provides resources for permit writers and regulators including training series and guidance documents to build capacity for Class VI permitting across the U.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA internal guidance to streamline permitting
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA issued internal guidelines intended to streamline and create uniformity and consistency in the Class VI permitting process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These guidelines set expectations for classification, project decision schedules, and target timeframes for components of permitting (public comment periods, response development, final decisions), and EPA will continue to evaluate processes for further improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms to identify, monitor, and mitigate induced seismicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Through the UIC Class VI program, EPA has mechanisms to identify, monitor, and mitigate risks associated with induced seismicity in and around sequestration sites, including site characterization and monitoring, and the requirement for applicants to demonstrate induced seismic activity will not endanger USDWs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If geologic/seismic data indicate substantial likelihood of seismic activity, additional analyses, planned operational changes, and augmented monitoring may be required. EPA may require seismic monitoring as a permit condition or deny a permit if injection-induced seismicity risk could endanger USDWs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority and practical approaches for injection-induced seismicity (Class II/VI)
rubrics_metrics.description: While UIC Class II lacks specific seismicity requirements, it provides discretionary authority to add conditions case-by-case; EPA produced guidance for UIC Directors on minimizing and managing injection-induced seismicity in Class II wells.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA references this practical guidance and indicates similar risk management approaches are available to protect USDWs across classes when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental justice and meaningful community engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA acknowledges the importance of meaningful engagement with historically disadvantaged and overburdened communities potentially impacted by geologic sequestration and has environmental justice guidance for Class VI permitting and primacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA expects Regions to apply these expectations broadly (including to other well classes where possible). See referenced section for detailed discussion of EJ requirements and guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: GHGRP reporting and leakage accounting (subpart RR and VV)
rubrics_metrics.description: GHGRP subpart RR and subpart VV regulations prescribe accounting methodologies for facilities to quantify and report any potential leakage at the surface; EPA makes sequestration data and related monitoring plans publicly available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule requires affected units that capture and inject CO2 underground to report under GHGRP subpart RR or VV. EPA differentiates its monitoring/reporting role from IRS tax credit administration (45Q). Reported emissions/leakage under subpart RR have been a small fraction (<0.5%) of sequestration volumes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to obtain Class VI permit when operations shift to sequestration
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations require the operator of a Class II well to obtain a Class VI permit when operations shift to geologic sequestration and there is consequently an increased risk to USDWs (40 CFR 144.19).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Class II wells are for oil and gas production fluids; when used for enhanced recovery or if operations shift to sequestration, Class VI permitting requirements apply to ensure protection of USDWs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class VI requirements for injection zone capacity and migration reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: UIC Class VI regulations require owners/operators to show the injection zone has sufficient volume to contain the injected CO2 stream and to report any fluid migration out of the injection zone and into or between USDWs (40 CFR 146.83 and 40 CFR 146.91).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These show-and-report obligations are central to permitting determinations and post-injection monitoring to protect USDWs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-injection site care (PISC) default period and monitoring obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Default time period for post-injection site care is 50 years, during which the permittee must monitor the position of the CO2 plume and pressure front and demonstrate that USDWs are not being endangered (40 CFR 146.93).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permittee must maintain financial responsibility to cover plugging, corrective action, emergency/remedial response, PISC, and site closure until permitting authority approves closure (40 CFR 146.85(a)&(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial responsibility and continued liability after operations
rubrics_metrics.description: The permittee generally must maintain financial responsibility sufficient to cover plugging, corrective actions, emergency/remedial response, PISC, and site closure; a former permittee may still be held liable for previous regulatory noncompliance and EPA may issue orders to protect public health (42 U.S.C. 300i; 40 CFR 144.12(e)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States are also enacting legislation addressing long-term liability; even after fulfilling UIC obligations, parties can be subject to enforcement if migration threatens USDWs.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA authority to require monitoring or deny permits for seismic risk
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA has the authority to require seismic monitoring as a condition of the UIC permit if appropriate, or to deny the permit if injection-induced seismicity risk could endanger USDWs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This authority is described alongside the site-characterization process that can trigger further analyses, operational changes, or additional monitoring when seismic risk indications exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitting experience and the impact of incomplete applications
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA disagrees that limited number of issued Class VI permits means lack of regulatory experience and emphasizes allocated resources to increase permitting efficiency; incomplete/insufficient materials can lead to substantially delayed permitting decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA recommends early contact with permitting authority to understand expectations and references a maintained list of UIC contacts; EPA has met with over 100 companies and stakeholders to assist potential applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: State primacy reduces EPA permit backlog
rubrics_metrics.description: If more states apply for and receive Class VI primacy, the number of permits in EPA review is expected to be reduced because states will review and issue permits under approved programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA transferred 56 Louisiana applications to the state once primacy effective; EPA continues to work with states developing primacy applications (e.g., Texas, Arizona, West Virginia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance date for CCS on long-term coal-fired units
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is finalizing a compliance date of January 1, 2032 for long-term coal-fired steam generating units subject to a CCS BSER, with a mechanism for a 1-year compliance date extension in cases with delays outside a source's control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justification assumes only initial feasibility work is done during the state plan development period and more substantial work begins after state plan submission; overall allows ~6 years 7 months for feasibility and substantial work post-rule issuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumed sequencing and durations for capture plant deployment
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's baseline (Sargent & Lundy) schedule assumes: 1 year FEED (June 2026–June 2027), up to 9 months commercial arrangements (June 2027–March 2028), 1 year permitting (Dec 2027–Dec 2028), 2 years engineering and procurement (March 2028–March 2030), sitework, 2 years construction, and ~14 months startup/commissioning, totaling ~5.78 years for final design, permitting, and installation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA notes many projects can compress timelines (e.g., expedite commercial arrangements, overlap permitting during FEED, reduce startup time) and incentives (e.g., 45Q/IRA) can accelerate deployment; EPA shows examples and concludes operation by Jan 1, 2032 is feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumed sequencing and durations for storage site and pipeline development
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA assumes substantial work on storage site begins June 2026 with 3 years for final site characterization, pore-space acquisition, and permitting (including at least 2 years for Class VI permitting), plus 1 year construction; pipeline substantial work lags storage by 6 months with up to 3 years for routing/permitting/right-of-way and 1.5 years for construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA assumes storage and pipeline installation can be performed concurrently with capture deployment; also notes at least an additional 12 months for sequestration construction is available without affecting other components.

rubrics_metrics.name: NEPA applicability and assumed durations
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA does not assume CCS projects are generally subject to NEPA; NEPA review is required when federal funding, federal lands, or triggers (e.g., CWA §404 permits) apply. An EA can take ~1 year; an EIS could take ~2 years and may be done concurrently with permitting/FEED.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA provides examples (Petra Nova) where NEPA processes overlapped FEED and were completed within ~2 years; NEPA review can begin prior to FEED in some circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of historical and modeling analyses to estimate affected coal capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: To estimate the inventory of coal-fired power plants potentially subject to CCS BSER, EPA uses multiple analyses: announced retirements, unit age distributions (average retirement age ~53 years), historical fleet trends (avg retirements ~8 GW/yr), and IPM baseline modeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining these lines of analysis, EPA considers ~42 GW of coal-fired generating capacity realistic to remain operating by 2039 and thus constitute affected sources for the long-term subcategory—but notes this is representative rather than a precise prediction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption that many sources may begin substantial CCS work after state plan submission
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA assumes feasibility work (~<1 year per component) occurs during state plan development and substantial work (e.g., FEED, permitting, ROW acquisition) resumes in June 2026 after state plan submission, though sources may start earlier if they choose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assumption underlies the compliance date justification but EPA recognizes some sources have ongoing FEED or are further advanced and can achieve operation earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default expectation that all affected units may need pipeline connections
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA conservatively assumes that all 81 GW of capacity with planned operation during/after 2039 would need to construct pipelines to connect to sequestration sites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA finalizes an exemption for coal-fired sources permanently ceasing operation by January 1, 2032; pipeline needs inform timelines and cost considerations in BSER analysis.
